You are a financial agent. You are given a question and you need to answer it using the tools provided.
You will not be able to interact with the user or ask clarifications, you must answer the question only based on the information provided.

You should answer all questions as if the current date is March 1, 2026.

You will have access to a data storage system. You can use this system to store parsed contents of HTML pages retrieved from the web.
You can then use the retrieve_information tool to answer questions or gather information from the stored documents using LLM-based prompts.
This data storage system is designed to help you avoid context window issues.

When you have the final answer, you should call the `submit_final_result` tool with it. Your submission will not be processed unless you call this tool.

You should include any necessary step-by-step reasoning, justification, calculations, or explanation in your answer. You will be evaluated both on the accuracy of the final answer, and the correctness of the supporting logic.

When possible, please provide any calculated answers to at least two decimal places (e.g. 18.78% rather than 19%). Please do not round intermediate steps in any calculations - you should only round your final answer.

SEC filings are the most authoritative source of financial data. If a number appears in both an SEC filing and another source (e.g., a press release or company website), use the SEC filing's figure.
You may freely use and cite non-SEC sources for information not available in SEC filings. For historical price data not available in SEC filings, use the `price_history` tool as your primary source. Fall back to `web_search` if the price tool is not working.
You should always use the raw, unadjusted price data from the `price_history` tool, unless the question specifically asks for the adjusted price.
Share prices should be reported in dollars with 2 decimal places, e.g. $10.25 per share.
Stock indices (^IXIC, ^GSPC, ^SOX, etc.) are not covered by `price_history` — for index historical levels, start with an authoritative source such as the data provided by FRED.
If the question references a specific source, make sure to incorporate information from that source, but still cross-reference SEC filings where relevant.

When reporting financial figures, use the same scale and units as presented in the SEC filing (e.g., if the filing reports values "in millions," report your answer in millions), unless otherwise specified in the question.

At the end of your answer, you should provide your sources in a dictionary with the following format:
{{
    "sources": [
        {{
            "url": "https://example.com",
            "name": "Name of the source"
        }},
        ...
    ]
}}

Question:
For NASDAQ:CRWD, in what ways does management believe Artificial Intelligence (AI) will serve as a tailwind to its current business, and what risks does management associate with AI? Base your answer on disclosures across the fiscal year ended January 31, 2025, and the period ended October 31, 2025.

tools.name: web_search

end_date.description: (optional) The end date for the search range in the format YYYY-MM-DD. If the value is later than 2026-03-01, it will be set to 2026-03-01.

number_of_results.description: (optional) The number of search results to return.

search_query.description: The query to search for

start_date.description: (optional) The start date for the search range in the format YYYY-MM-DD. Must not be equal to end_date.

tools.description: Search the public internet for information. Each result will contain a url, a title, and one excerpt taken directly from the page.

tools.name: retrieve_information

input_character_ranges.description: An optional list of character range specifications for extracting only portions of documents. Each object should have 'key' (the document key), 'start' (start character index, inclusive), and 'end' (end character index, exclusive). By default, the full document is used if this parameter is not provided or if a key is not included in the list.

key.description: The document key from data storage

prompt.description: The prompt that will be passed to the LLM. You MUST include at least one data storage key in the format {{key_name}} - for example: 'Summarize this 10-K filing: {{company_10k}}'. The content stored under each key will replace the {{key_name}} placeholder.

tools.description:
This tool allows you to retrieve data from previously saved documents from the agent's data storage system, by applying an LLM prompt to the stored document.

To use the tool, you will need to provide a prompt. This prompt will include both the query to be sent to the LLM, as well as the keys of files you have previously saved to the data storage system.

For example, if you want to analyze data stored under the key "financial_report", your prompt should look like the following:
"Analyze the following financial report and extract the revenue figures: {{financial_report}}"

The {{key_name}} will be replaced with the full text of the document stored under that key before the query is sent.

IMPORTANT: Your prompt MUST include at least one key from the data storage using this exact format: {{key_name}}. If you don't use this exact format with double braces, the tool will fail to retrieve the information.

You can also optionally only pass *a portion* of each document to the LLM, rather than the entire document. This can be used to avoid token limit errors or improve efficiency. To do so, use the input_character_ranges parameter to specify which portions of documents to extract. For example, if "financial_report" contains "Annual Report 2023" and you specify:  [{"key": "financial_report", "start": 1, "end": 6}], then only "nnual" will be inserted into the prompt (characters 1 through 5, as end is exclusive).

tools.name: parse_html_page

key.description: The key to use when saving the result in the conversation's data storage.

url.description: The URL of the HTML page to parse

tools.description: This tool is used to parse the contents of an HTML page and save it to the agent's data storage system. The tool will retrieve the HTML page from the URL provided, then parse it from HTML to plain text. Finally, it will save it to the agent's data storage system under the key provided. You can use the retrieve_information tool to later retrieve information about the stored page.

tools.name: edgar_search

ciks.description: (optional) Filters results to filings from specified CIKs, type list of strings. Leading zeros are optional but may be included. Example: [ "0001811414", "1318605" ]. Default: all CIKs

end_date.description: (optional) End date for the search range, in the same format as startDate. If the value is a date that is later than 2026-03-01, it will be set to 2026-03-01.

form_types.description: (optional) Limits search to specific EDGAR form types (e.g., ['8-K', '10-Q']) list of strings. Default: all form types

page.description: (optional) Used for pagination. Each page contains up to 100 matching filings. Increase the page number to retrieve the next set of 100 filings. Example: 3 retrieves the third page. Default: 1

search_query.description: The case-insensitive search-term or phrase to search the contents of filings and their attachments. This can be a single word, phrase, or combination of words and phrases. Supported search features include wildcards (*), Boolean operators (OR, NOT), and exact phrase matching by enclosing phrases in quotation marks ("exact phrase"). By default, all terms are joined by an implicit AND operator.

start_date.description: (optional) Start date for the search range in yyyy-mm-dd format. If the value is a date that is later than 2026-03-01, it will be set to 2026-03-01.

top_n_results.description: (optional) Return only the first N results out of 100 from the page. If not provided, all 100 results will be returned. E.g. if page is 2, and top_n_results is 10, you will receive results 100 to 110.

tools.description: Search the EDGAR Database through the SEC API. You should provide a search query. You can also optionally provide a start date, an end date, a page number, top N results, a list of form types, and/or a list of CIKs. The results are returned as a list of dictionaries, each containing the metadata for a filing. It does not contain the full text of the filing.

Supports: +, -, *, /, ** (exponentiation), % (modulo), and parentheses for grouping. Available functions: abs(), min(), max(), sqrt(), log(), log10(). Examples: '(5000 - 3200) * 0.21', '(2865507 / 1905871) ** 0.5 - 1', '14060 / 2148'.

asset_class.description: Asset class used to route to the proper pricing endpoint.

end_date.description: End date YYYY-MM-DD (inclusive).

start_date.description: Start date YYYY-MM-DD (inclusive).

ticker.description: Ticker symbol. High-level symbology rules: (1) Equity/ETF/mutual fund: use the US exchange-listed symbol (AAPL, SPY, VFIAX). Symbols are case-insensitive and contain only letters and dashes. (2) Share classes use a dash, not a dot: 'BRK-A' / 'BRK-B' (not 'BRK.A'), 'BF-B'. (3) Securities are identified by the ticker as listed on the primary US exchange; non-US listings, OTC pink sheets, indices, and futures are generally not covered. (4) Tickers can be reused after delisting; data is point-in-time for the entity that held the ticker on each date. (5) Crypto: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'btcusd', 'ethusd'. (6) FX: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'audusd', 'eurusd'.

tools.description: Fetch historical daily price data for a specific asset class. Returns a CSV table with one row per day. Use asset_class='equity' or 'etf' for US-listed stocks/ETFs (e.g. AAPL, SPY), 'crypto' for pairs like btcusd (lowercase, no dash), or 'fx' for pairs like audusd. Non-US equities and most indices/futures are not covered by the pricing provider. Each row includes raw OHLC (open/high/low/close), split- and dividend-adjusted OHLC (adjOpen/adjHigh/adjLow/adjClose), raw and adjusted volume, divCash (dividend amount on the date), and splitFactor.

{"results":"## CrowdStrike FY2025 Form 10-K — AI-related disclosures

The filing discusses AI primarily in three contexts: **(1) product architecture and benefits, (2) AI-related market opportunities and adversary threats, and (3) legal, technical, competitive and operational risks.** No separate AI revenue, bookings, ARR, or profitability amount is disclosed.

---

# A. Company strategy, platform architecture and product benefits

## 1. Overview — AI-native Falcon platform and Security Cloud  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Business—Overview,” p. 4; repeated in Part II, Item 7, “MD&A—Overview,” p. 61.

CrowdStrike states that it “reinvented cybersecurity for the cloud and artificial intelligence (‘AI’) era” and describes Falcon as an **“AI-native” cloud platform with AI at its core**.

Key disclosures:

- Falcon can harness large volumes of security and enterprise data through a single lightweight agent.
- CrowdStrike uses collected data to **train AI to detect and prevent threats** and to automate workflows, giving security teams “machine speed advantage.”
- Its Security Cloud uses “cloud-scale AI” to enrich and correlate **trillions of cybersecurity events per week** with attack indicators, threat intelligence and enterprise data.
- The resulting data is used to:
  - create actionable information;
  - identify changes in adversary tactics; and
  - automatically prevent threats in real time.
- CrowdStrike says that the more data fed into Falcon, the more intelligent the Security Cloud becomes, producing a network effect that increases customer value.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and strategic opportunity.

---

## 2. Falcon architecture and AI-enabled modules  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “The Architectural Purpose Behind the Platform,” pp. 4–5.

CrowdStrike says Falcon was purpose-built in the cloud to use data and AI to deliver automated protection and provide threat hunters with intelligence needed to stop sophisticated attacks, including malware-free and fileless attacks.

The company identifies “AI powered workflow automation” and “securing generative AI workloads” among Falcon’s security and IT markets.

It also states that the lightweight agent:

- ingests data once and streams high-fidelity data to the Security Cloud;
- reuses the data for multiple use cases;
- continuously improves Falcon’s AI algorithms; and
- makes real-time decision-making “faster and smarter” as adversary tactics change.

**Classification:** Company product benefit.

---

## 3. Threat Graph, AI algorithms and proprietary data advantage  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Technology” and “Threat Graph,” pp. 11–12.

CrowdStrike describes the Threat Graph as using **AI and behavioral pattern matching** to correlate and analyze cybersecurity events and identify linked threat activity.

The filing says Threat Graph:

- tracks process and software behavior rather than relying only on file characteristics;
- enriches data with threat intelligence;
- applies graph analytics and AI algorithms to identify relationships among events that may otherwise indicate an undetected attack;
- provides real-time and historical visibility for threat hunting; and
- supports rapid creation of new cloud modules through reusable data, correlation and action capabilities.

CrowdStrike says its AI algorithms are advantaged by the “rich proprietary dataset” used to train them.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and competitive differentiator.

---

## 4. Cloud-scale AI as a competitive differentiator  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “The Architectural Purpose Behind the Platform,” p. 5.

The filing states that AI effectiveness depends on the **quality and volume of training data** and on selecting the right features from that data.

CrowdStrike says its Security Cloud has:

- a large, high-fidelity, crowdsourced dataset;
- continuous AI-model training;
- deep human cybersecurity expertise; and
- a combination that supports high efficacy and low false positives.

It argues that its cloud-native architecture allows AI algorithms to operate at cloud scale and detect and prevent threats more effectively than on-premise, cloud-hosted or hybrid products whose architectures limit data storage and analysis.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and competitive advantage.

---

## 5. “Power of the Crowd” and network effects  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Built for This Moment and the Future—Key benefits,” p. 7.

CrowdStrike says that as customers contribute more high-fidelity data to the Security Cloud, its AI models continue to train and improve, increasing the overall efficacy of Falcon.

The filing characterizes the data layer, Threat Graph, Intel Graph and Asset Graph as mechanisms that put threats, adversaries and assets into context for rapid security decisions.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and opportunity.

---

## 6. AI innovation, Charlotte AI and agentic cybersecurity  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Built for This Moment and the Future—Key benefits,” p. 7.

CrowdStrike says it is a pioneer in using AI to transform cybersecurity, combining:

- “AI for cybersecurity”; and
- “cybersecurity for AI.”

The filing specifically states that:

- Falcon’s AI-native architecture and Security Cloud help detect and stop breaches.
- **Charlotte AI** represents an advance in “agentic AI.”
- Charlotte AI can make autonomous security decisions within customer-defined guardrails.
- It is designed to triage detections, reduce noise and accelerate response.
- High-fidelity data and continual training allow Charlotte AI to reduce routine investigation workloads and help address cybersecurity skills shortages.
- CrowdStrike is pursuing AI-powered agentic cybersecurity in which AI can act independently while preserving human oversight and control.
- The company also helps customers secure AI systems, including generative AI applications, sensitive data, AI configurations and AI vulnerabilities.

CrowdStrike links these capabilities to greater operational efficiency and the ability to adopt AI more securely.

**Classification:** Company product benefits, current-business tailwind and growth opportunity.

---

## 7. AI-related platform expansion and productivity  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “The Falcon Platform: Built to Innovate and Scale,” p. 9.

CrowdStrike says that unifying data from its modules and customers in one cloud infrastructure gives it an advantage in:

- developing and delivering AI capabilities to detect and prevent threats; and
- improving productivity and efficiency through generative AI systems such as Charlotte AI.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and platform expansion opportunity.

---

## 8. AI-related product disclosures  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “CrowdStrike Falcon Platform: Unified Security Across Major Categories,” pp. 9–10.

### Next-Generation SIEM and Log Management

CrowdStrike describes its Next-Gen SIEM and log-management offerings as providing **AI-driven detection, investigation and response**, alongside high-performance log management.

**Classification:** Company product benefit.

### Generative AI / Charlotte AI

The filing says Charlotte AI uses generative AI and natural-language processing to automate time-intensive tasks. It is intended to:

- improve analyst efficiency;
- turn hours of routine investigation into minutes;
- address cybersecurity skills shortages; and
- provide time savings and workflow automation.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and opportunity.

### Falcon for IT

CrowdStrike says Falcon for IT uses **generative AI workflows and automation** to streamline IT processes, resolve operational issues and maintain a secure infrastructure.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and adjacent-market opportunity.

### Data Protection

The company says Falcon Data Protection addresses “the unique risks of the GenAI era” by providing visibility into sensitive-data movement across endpoints, web applications, cloud drives and USB storage.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and AI-related demand opportunity.

### Managed services

Falcon Complete Next-Gen MDR is described as being powered by the AI-native Falcon platform and combined with expert monitoring, investigation, response and remediation.

**Classification:** Company product benefit.

---

## 9. Machine learning and autonomous endpoint protection  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Technology—Falcon Agent,” p. 11.

The Falcon agent uses:

- machine learning;
- AI;
- exploit blocking; and
- behavioral techniques

to identify and prevent known and unknown malware and fileless attacks.

The agent can:

- act autonomously;
- continue protecting endpoints while offline;
- use local situational models;
- analyze events through agent-based AI models;
- take preventative and responsive actions automatically or under human control; and
- receive real-time configuration changes based on cloud analytics.

**Classification:** Company product benefit.

---

## 10. Local machine learning and smart filtering  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Technology—High Fidelity Data and Smart Filtering,” p. 12.

The local graph model in the Falcon agent supports:

- rapid machine learning;
- behavioral analysis;
- tracking machine state in real time; and
- efficient event streaming.

CrowdStrike says the agent analyzes unfiltered data locally but sends only high-fidelity events to the cloud. This “smart filtering” is intended to:

- minimize endpoint performance overhead;
- reduce bandwidth requirements;
- process large data volumes efficiently; and
- separate signals from noise.

**Classification:** Company product and operational benefit.

---

## 11. AI red-teaming and professional services  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Professional Services—Technical Assessment and Strategic Advisory Services,” p. 13.

CrowdStrike says it has added **AI red-teaming** to help customers:

- understand where AI models may create risk;
- identify how those models could be exploited; and
- determine corrective security actions.

**Classification:** Company product benefit and AI-security opportunity.

---

## 12. AI-related corporate and research mission  
**Section:** Part I, Item 1, “Information about Executive Officers,” pp. 19–20.

The CrowdStrike Foundation is described as supporting the next generation of talent and research in **cybersecurity and artificial intelligence** through scholarships, grants and other activities.

**Classification:** Corporate/strategic AI-related activity; not a product or financial disclosure.

---

## 13. AI-native platform in financial-statement business description  
**Section:** Part II, Item 8, Note 1, “Description of Business and Significant Accounting Policies—Business,” p. 85.

The company describes itself as delivering “cybersecurity’s AI-native platform for the XDR era.” Its SaaS platform includes cybersecurity generative AI among its markets.

{"final_result":"For CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), management presents AI as both a **core capability already embedded in Falcon** and a **driver of additional cybersecurity demand**. The fiscal-2025 Form 10-K and the Form 10-Q for the period ended October 31, 2025 describe the following.

## How management believes AI is a tailwind

1. **AI improves Falcon’s threat detection and prevention.**  CrowdStrike describes Falcon as an “AI-native” cloud platform with AI at its core. Its Security Cloud uses cloud-scale AI to process and correlate trillions of cybersecurity events weekly with indicators of attack, threat intelligence and enterprise data. Management says this helps identify changing adversary tactics, generate actionable intelligence and automatically prevent threats in real time.

2. **The platform benefits from a data/network effect.**  Falcon collects data through a single lightweight agent and uses that data to train and improve its AI models. Management says that the more high-fidelity data fed into the Security Cloud, the more intelligent it becomes, increasing the value and efficacy of Falcon for customers. CrowdStrike views its proprietary, continuously expanding dataset as a competitive advantage because AI effectiveness depends heavily on the quality and volume of training data.

3. **AI supports protection against more sophisticated attacks.**  The 10-K says the commoditization of generative AI is allowing less-skilled adversaries to launch faster and more sophisticated attacks, including social-engineering, identity/credential and non-malware attacks. Management therefore sees AI-driven threat complexity as a tailwind to demand for cybersecurity products capable of behavioral analysis and real-time response—not merely signature-based malware detection.

4. **AI can expand customer productivity and security-team capacity.**  CrowdStrike’s Charlotte AI uses generative AI and natural-language processing to automate investigation and response tasks, reduce alert noise and turn time-intensive work into much faster workflows. Management believes this can improve analyst productivity, help address cybersecurity-staffing shortages and enable agentic cybersecurity—AI making autonomous decisions within customer-defined guardrails while retaining human oversight.

5. **AI broadens the Falcon platform’s product and market opportunity.**  The filings identify cybersecurity generative AI as a market served by Falcon. Examples include AI-driven detection, investigation and response in Next-Gen SIEM; generative-AI workflows in Falcon for IT; and Falcon Data Protection, which addresses sensitive-data movement and other risks arising in the generative-AI era. CrowdStrike also offers AI red-teaming to help customers identify how AI models might be exploited and how to remediate those risks.

6. **AI can support adjacent-market expansion and investment.**  In the October 2025 10-Q, CrowdStrike disclosed its acquisition of Pangea Cyber Corporation, an AI detection-and-response provider. Management said the acquisition’s goodwill reflected, among other things, planned growth in new markets and expected integration synergies. The company also identified AI-related infrastructure and technology investment as necessary to support customer growth and service delivery.

Thus, management’s basic thesis is that AI is a two-sided business tailwind: it makes CrowdStrike’s own platform more effective and efficient, while simultaneously making the threat environment more dangerous and increasing customers’ need for security, AI protection and automated response. The filings do not quantify a separate AI contribution to revenue, ARR, margins or growth.

## Risks management associates with AI

1. **Unreliable or harmful outputs.**  Generative AI may produce false or “hallucinatory” inferences or outputs. Machine-learning and predictive-analytics systems may be flawed, insufficient, low quality, biased or contain errors that are difficult to detect. If customers rely on flawed output, CrowdStrike could face reputational, competitive or legal harm.

2. **Product-efficacy limitations.**  AI-enabled security may fail to detect or prevent advanced, novel or rapidly changing attacks, and may produce false positives. CrowdStrike emphasizes that no security solution, including Falcon, can address every possible threat. AI improves defenses but does not eliminate the possibility of a breach or a customer perception that Falcon failed.

3. **AI-enhanced attacks against CrowdStrike and its customers.**  Threat actors may use AI to increase the frequency or effectiveness of malware, hacking, fraudulent-use attempts and phishing. Such attacks could cause service interruptions, data breaches, loss of critical data, development delays and reputational damage.

4. **Competitive risk.**  AI is developing rapidly, and competitors may incorporate it more quickly or effectively, obtain superior access to AI technologies or achieve greater market acceptance. The resulting effects could include loss of market share, pricing pressure, fewer orders, lower revenue and gross margins, and greater losses.

5. **Regulatory uncertainty and compliance costs.**  AI may be regulated under intellectual-property, privacy and data-protection, cybersecurity, consumer-protection, competition and equal-opportunity laws. Across the two filings, CrowdStrike cites the EU AI Act and U.S. state initiatives, including California laws concerning transparency, privacy and fairness, as well as Colorado and Utah legislation. Rules may evolve quickly and differ by jurisdiction, requiring product changes, increased operating expenses and potentially limiting how products can be offered or used.

6. **Data, privacy, intellectual-property and contractual exposure.**  CrowdStrike may not possess sufficient rights to use data, content or other material on which its AI systems rely. That could result in claims involving third-party intellectual property, privacy, other rights, contracts or applicable laws. AI-generated output may also not qualify for copyright protection, potentially weakening the company’s ability to protect its own intellectual property.

7. **Ethical, social and reputational risk.**  AI products or uses may provoke ethical or social controversy or regulatory scrutiny because of their perceived or actual effects on customers or society. That could delay purchasing decisions and cause brand, competitive or legal harm.

8. **Execution and return-on-investment risk.**  The October 2025 10-Q more explicitly notes that incorporating AI, including generative AI, requires significant resources and that investments may not deliver expected benefits. AI-related infrastructure may be complex, new, untested or difficult to scale, and CrowdStrike may fail to implement it successfully, forecast demand accurately or achieve expected results.

9. **Unknown risks.**  Because AI is complex and rapidly evolving, management says it cannot predict all of the legal, operational and technological risks that may arise.

### Bottom line

Management views AI as a net opportunity for the current business because it strengthens Falcon’s detection, prevention, automation and analyst-productivity capabilities; creates demand for securing AI applications and data; and expands CrowdStrike into related products and markets. However, the same technology increases competitive pressure, introduces reliability and liability concerns, creates data-rights and regulatory uncertainty, requires substantial investment, and gives attackers additional tools. The October 2025 disclosure is broadly consistent with the 10-K but adds greater emphasis on the costs and execution risk of AI investment, the expanding regulatory landscape and the Pangea AI-detection acquisition.

Examples include AI-driven detection, investigation and response in Next-Gen SIEM; generative-AI workflows in Falcon for IT; and Falcon Data Protection, which addresses sensitive-data movement and other risks arising in the generative-AI era. CrowdStrike also offers AI red-teaming to help customers identify how AI models might be exploited and how to remediate those risks.

6. **AI can support adjacent-market expansion and investment.**  In the October 2025 10-Q, CrowdStrike disclosed its acquisition of Pangea Cyber Corporation, an AI detection-and-response provider. Management said the acquisition’s goodwill reflected, among other things, planned growth in new markets and expected integration synergies. The company also identified AI-related infrastructure and technology investment as necessary to support customer growth and service delivery.

Thus, management’s basic thesis is that AI is a two-sided business tailwind: it makes CrowdStrike’s own platform more effective and efficient, while simultaneously making the threat environment more dangerous and increasing customers’ need for security, AI protection and automated response. The filings do not quantify a separate AI contribution to revenue, ARR, margins or growth.

## Risks management associates with AI

1. **Unreliable or harmful outputs.**  Generative AI may produce false or “hallucinatory” inferences or outputs. Machine-learning and predictive-analytics systems may be flawed, insufficient, low quality, biased or contain errors that are difficult to detect. If customers rely on flawed output, CrowdStrike could face reputational, competitive or legal harm.

2. **Product-efficacy limitations.**  AI-enabled security may fail to detect or prevent advanced, novel or rapidly changing attacks, and may produce false positives. CrowdStrike emphasizes that no security solution, including Falcon, can address every possible threat. AI improves defenses but does not eliminate the possibility of a breach or a customer perception that Falcon failed.

3. **AI-enhanced attacks against CrowdStrike and its customers.**  Threat actors may use AI to increase the frequency or effectiveness of malware, hacking, fraudulent-use attempts and phishing. Such attacks could cause service interruptions, data breaches, loss of critical data, development delays and reputational damage.

4. **Competitive risk.**  AI is developing rapidly, and competitors may incorporate it more quickly or effectively, obtain superior access to AI technologies or achieve greater market acceptance. The resulting effects could include loss of market share, pricing pressure, fewer orders, lower revenue and gross margins, and greater losses.

5. **Regulatory uncertainty and compliance costs.**  AI may be regulated under intellectual-property, privacy and data-protection, cybersecurity, consumer-protection, competition and equal-opportunity laws. Across the two filings, CrowdStrike cites the EU AI Act and U.S. state initiatives, including California laws concerning transparency, privacy and fairness, as well as Colorado and Utah legislation. Rules may evolve quickly and differ by jurisdiction, requiring product changes, increased operating expenses and potentially limiting how products can be offered or used.

6. **Data, privacy, intellectual-property and contractual exposure.**  CrowdStrike may not possess sufficient rights to use data, content or other material on which its AI systems rely. That could result in claims involving third-party intellectual property, privacy, other rights, contracts or applicable laws. AI-generated output may also not qualify for copyright protection, potentially weakening the company’s ability to protect its own intellectual property.

7. **Ethical, social and reputational risk.**  AI products or uses may provoke ethical or social controversy or regulatory scrutiny because of their perceived or actual effects on customers or society. That could delay purchasing decisions and cause brand, competitive or legal harm.

8. **Execution and return-on-investment risk.**  The October 2025 10-Q more explicitly notes that incorporating AI, including generative AI, requires significant resources and that investments may not deliver expected benefits. AI-related infrastructure may be complex, new, untested or difficult to scale, and CrowdStrike may fail to implement it successfully, forecast demand accurately or achieve expected results.

9. **Unknown risks.**  Because AI is complex and rapidly evolving, management says it cannot predict all of the legal, operational and technological risks that may arise.

### Bottom line

Management views AI as a net opportunity for the current business because it strengthens Falcon’s detection, prevention, automation and analyst-productivity capabilities; creates demand for securing AI applications and data; and expands CrowdStrike into related products and markets. However, the same technology increases competitive pressure, introduces reliability and liability concerns, creates data-rights and regulatory uncertainty, requires substantial investment, and gives attackers additional tools. The October 2025 disclosure is broadly consistent with the 10-K but adds greater emphasis on the costs and execution risk of AI investment, the expanding regulatory landscape and the Pangea AI-detection acquisition.

(4) Tickers can be reused after delisting; data is point-in-time for the entity that held the ticker on each date. (5) Crypto: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'btcusd', 'ethusd'. (6) FX: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'audusd', 'eurusd'.

tools.description: Fetch historical daily price data for a specific asset class. Returns a CSV table with one row per day. {"results":"## Marriott Bonvoy loyalty disclosures in the FY2025 Form 10-K

### 1. Loyalty-member room-night percentages

**FY2025 booking penetration — Part I, Item 1, “Loyalty and Credit Card Programs,” p. 8**

Marriott states:

> “In 2025, approximately **75 percent of our U.S. hotel room nights** and approximately **68 percent of our global hotel room nights** were booked by Loyalty Program members.”

- **Period:** Fiscal year 2025.
- **U.S. denominator:** Total U.S. hotel room nights.
- **Global denominator:** Total global hotel room nights.
- **Numerical denominators:** The filing does **not** provide the underlying number of U.S. or global hotel room nights, nor the corresponding member-booked room-night counts. It reports only the approximate percentages.
- The filing does not state whether the percentages are based on comparable properties, systemwide properties, occupied rooms, or another narrower population; it describes them generally as “our U.S. hotel room nights” and “our global hotel room nights.”

Marriott says it believes the program generates “substantial repeat business that might otherwise go to competing properties,” and that it markets to the “large and growing guest base” to generate revenue and attract and enroll new members (p. 8).

---

### 2. Membership and member activity

#### Membership size

The FY2025 Form 10-K does **not disclose a numerical Marriott Bonvoy membership count**.

It describes the membership base qualitatively as:

> “this large and growing guest base”

and says Marriott is:

> “focused on attracting and enrolling new Loyalty Program members.”

**Context:** Part I, Item 1, “Loyalty and Credit Card Programs,” p. 8.

#### How members earn points

**Note 2, “Loyalty Program,” pp. 41–42; Part I, Item 1, p. 8**

Members earn points through:

- spending at participating properties;
- stays at participating properties;
- exchange of timeshare ownership interests;
- purchases of timeshare intervals, fractional ownership, and residential products;
- participation in travel experiences;
- affiliated partner programs, including credit-card, car-rental, airline, and other companies;
- purchases using Marriott Bonvoy co-branded credit cards; and
- other travel offerings, including Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy.

The business section summarizes that members can earn points through:

> “stays at participating properties and other travel offerings, such as Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy … as well as through purchases with co-branded credit cards and our Loyalty Program partners.”

#### How members redeem points

Members may redeem points for:

- stays at participating properties;
- airline tickets;
- airline frequent-flyer-program miles;
- rental cars;
- merchandise and products from Marriott Bonvoy Boutiques;
- gift cards and other awards; and
- experiences through Marriott Bonvoy Moments.

The filing also says:

> “Points cannot be redeemed for cash.”

**Context:** Part I, Item 1, p. 8; Note 2, pp. 41–42.

#### Loyalty Program accounting balances and activity

**Note 2, “Contract Balances,” p. 42; Consolidated Balance Sheets, p. 37; Statement of Cash Flows, p. 38**

Marriott reports:

- **Liability for guest loyalty program at December 31, 2025:** **$7,992 million**
  - Current portion: **$3,497 million**
  - Long-term portion: **$4,495 million**
- **December 31, 2024 liability:** **$7,519 million**
- The liability increased **$473 million**, primarily reflecting points earned by members.
- The increase was partially offset by **$3,160 million** of revenue recognized in 2025 that had been deferred at December 31, 2024.
- Updated estimates in 2025 caused a **net decrease in revenue and corresponding increase in the liability of approximately $102 million**.

The 2025 Statement of Cash Flows also shows a **$473 million increase in the liability for guest loyalty program** in operating activities (p. 38).

The critical audit matter disclosure states that during 2025 Marriott recognized **$3,160 million** of revenue previously deferred at December 31, 2024 and had **$7,992 million of deferred revenue** associated with the Loyalty Program at December 31, 2025. In that audit disclosure, “deferred revenue” refers to the loyalty-program-related deferred balance described in Note 2 (pp. 33–34).

---

## 3. Funding and economic mechanisms

### A. Hotel-owner reimbursement of Loyalty Program costs

**Part I, Item 1, “Franchised, Licensed, and Other Properties,” p. 7; “Company-Operated Properties,” p. 7; Note 2, pp. 40–42**

For franchised hotels, Marriott generally receives:

> “reimbursement for centralized programs and services, such as our Loyalty Program, reservations, and marketing.”

For managed hotels, Marriott provides centralized programs including the Loyalty Program, and:

> “Under our management agreements, hotel owners are generally responsible for hotel operating costs, including centralized programs and services.”

Note 2 provides the more specific mechanism:

> “Our agreements with hotel owners and certain other counterparties require that properties reimburse us for costs of operating the Loyalty Program, with no added mark-up.”

The reimbursable costs include:

- marketing;
- promotion;
- communications; and
- services provided to Loyalty Program members.

Marriott expenses those costs as incurred in **“Reimbursed expenses.”**

Marriott generally receives:

> “monthly cash contributions from participating properties based on a portion of qualified spend by Loyalty Program members (when the points are earned).”

It recognizes those contributions as revenue when the related service is provided—generally:

> “when the points are redeemed.”

Thus, the filing describes an owner/property funding model in which participating properties contribute based on qualified member spending, while Marriott operates the program and initially incurs specified program costs.

#### No-mark-up reimbursement model generally

**Note 2, p. 40; MD&A, p. 25**

Marriott explains that costs incurred on behalf of hotel owners and other counterparties are generally reimbursed **with no added mark-up**. Centralized programs and services, including marketing, sales, reservations, insurance, and Loyalty Program-related services, are:

> “not designed to impact our economics, either positively or negatively”  
> over the long term.

For 2025, consolidated cost-reimbursement amounts were:

- **Cost reimbursement revenue:** **$19,204 million**
- **Reimbursed expenses:** **$19,503 million**
- **Cost reimbursements, net:** **$(299) million**

The filing says the change in net cost reimbursements primarily reflected higher Loyalty Program revenues, partially offset by higher expenses, net of revenues, for other programs and services. It does not separately disclose total 2025 Loyalty Program revenue, total Loyalty Program expense, or the amount reimbursed specifically by hotel owners for Loyalty Program costs.

### B. Point-redemption economics

**Note 2, p. 41**

Marriott has a performance obligation to:

> “provide or arrange for the provision of goods or services to Loyalty Program members in exchange for the redemption of points earned from past activities.”

Marriott recognizes revenue when points are redeemed and the related performance obligation is satisfied. The revenue amount is based on:

- a blend of historical funding rates; and
- the estimated “breakage” of points that members will never redeem.

Marriott states:

> “We recognize revenue net of the redemption cost … as our performance obligation is to facilitate the transaction between the Loyalty Program member and the property or program partner.”

It also cautions:

> “Our redemption cost could be higher or lower than our revenue recognized in any given period.”

Accordingly, Marriott presents itself primarily as facilitating the redemption transaction between the member and the hotel, program partner, or other provider, rather than recognizing the gross redemption-related amount as revenue.

The filing does not expressly state that Marriott itself bears all redemption costs. Instead, it says:

- participating properties reimburse Marriott for specified program-operating costs with no mark-up;
- Marriott recognizes revenue net of redemption cost; and
- the performance obligation is to facilitate the transaction between the member and the property or program partner.

### C. Breakage and redemption estimates

**Note 2, p. 41; MD&A, p. 28; Critical Audit Matter, pp. 33–34**

Marriott estimates the portion of points that will never be redeemed based on:

> “historical member activity and expectations of future member behavior.”

The estimate affects the timing and amount of revenue recognition. The filing identifies the following as significant estimates:

- breakage of hotel points;
- breakage of credit-card points;
- breakage of free-night certificates;
- the volume of points and certificates issued;
- consideration expected under co-branded-card agreements; and
- standalone selling prices of goods and services provided under those agreements.

Sensitivity disclosure:

> “A one percent decrease in our estimate of the breakage of points could result in an increase in the liability for guest loyalty program of approximately **$50 million**.”

Marriott says the effect may vary significantly depending on the specific points involved.

### D. Co-branded credit cards

**Part I, Item 1, pp. 8–9; Note 2, pp. 41–42**

Marriott has co-branded credit cards associated with Marriott Bonvoy in **11 countries**.

In the United States, Marriott has multi-year agreements with:

- **JPMorgan Chase**
- **American Express**

Internationally, it licenses credit-card programs in markets including:

- Japan;
- the United Arab Emirates;
- China;
- Canada; and
- other markets.

Marriott generally receives:

- fixed amounts payable primarily at contract inception; and
- variable monthly amounts over the contract term, primarily based on card usage.

Note 2 specifies that variable consideration generally depends on:

1. cardholder spending volume;
2. the number of Loyalty Program points purchased;
3. the number of free-night certificates issued or redeemed; and
4. the number of gift cards issued.

Marriott states:

> “Payments received under our co-branded credit card agreements represent a significant funding source for the Loyalty Program.”

It also says the cards create a diversified revenue stream and provide value to:

- Marriott;
- guests;
- hotel owners; and
- other affiliated parties.

#### Credit-card performance obligations and revenue allocation

Under the co-branded-card agreements, Marriott has performance obligations to:

- license brand intellectual property and marketing lists to issuing financial institutions;
- arrange for redemption of Loyalty Program points;
- arrange for redemption of free-night certificates; and
- arrange for redemption of gift cards provided to cardholders.

Marriott allocates credit-card fees among those obligations based on estimated standalone selling prices. It recognizes:

- sales-based Licensed IP revenue as the cards are used;
- remaining Licensed IP revenue on a straight-line basis over the contract term;
- points-related revenue when points are redeemed;
- free-night-certificate and gift-card revenue when the related service is provided; and
- revenue net of redemption cost.

Licensed IP revenue is recorded primarily in **“Franchise fees,”** with a portion recorded in **“Cost reimbursement revenue.”**

The filing does not separately disclose the dollar amount of co-branded-card fees or the portion of total Loyalty Program funding supplied by card issuers.

### E. Licensing, franchise, and other fees connected with Bonvoy

**Part I, Item 1, pp. 7–9; MD&A, p. 22; Note 14, pp. 58–59**

Marriott’s hotel franchise arrangements generally provide for:

- initial application fees;
- continuing room royalty fees, typically **4% to 7% of room revenues**;
- for certain brands, up to **4% of food-and-beverage revenues**; and
- reimbursement for centralized programs and services, including the Loyalty Program.

Certain licensees and other counterparties are also charged for centralized programs such as:

- the Loyalty Program;
- reservations; and
- marketing.

Marriott has license and other arrangements for offerings including:

- timeshare properties;
- MGM Collection with Marriott Bonvoy;
- Design Hotels; and
- The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection.

Under those arrangements Marriott receives royalty and other fees, and certain counterparties may be charged for Loyalty Program-related systems and centralized services.

The MD&A also says Marriott earns fees for other uses of its intellectual property, including primarily:

> “co-branded credit card fees, as well as residential branding fees and certain other licensing fees.”

In segment reporting, Marriott says that **“Unallocated corporate and other”** includes:

- fees received from credit-card programs;
- timeshare licensing revenues;
- revenues and expenses for the Loyalty Program; and
- other items not allocated to reportable operating segments.

The filing does not provide a separate line item for total Loyalty Program licensing fees, total Bonvoy-related fee revenue, or total fees paid by each type of licensee.

### F. Who bears the costs

Based on the disclosures:

- **Hotel owners/participating properties:** Generally bear hotel operating costs and reimburse Marriott for specified centralized-program and Loyalty Program costs, with no added mark-up. Contributions are generally based partly on qualified member spend.
- **Marriott:** Operates the Loyalty Program, incurs the specified program costs initially, provides or arranges member rewards, performs the accounting, and recognizes related revenue net of redemption cost.
- **Co-branded-card issuing financial institutions:** Pay Marriott fixed and variable contractual amounts. Those payments are described as a significant source of Loyalty Program funding.
- **Program partners/property operators:** Participate in providing the goods or services redeemed by members; Marriott describes its performance obligation as facilitating the transaction between the member and the property or program partner.
- **Marriott’s own economics:** Centralized programs are generally intended to be reimbursed over the long term and are not designed to produce a profit or loss for Marriott. Timing differences can nevertheless cause annual net cost reimbursements to be positive or negative.

The filing does not quantify the relative share of funding borne by hotel owners, card issuers, Marriott, or other program partners, and it does not state that one party bears all reward-redemption costs.

### G. Other relevant program disclosures

**Risk Factors, pp. 14 and 18**

Marriott says the Loyalty Program is an important aspect of its business and faces competition from hospitality companies, banks, airlines, and others. Its competitive factors include:

- value and utility of program currency;
- reward ranges and values;
- program terms and conditions;
- program features; and
- co-branded credit-card affiliations and offerings.

The filing warns that regulatory changes affecting credit-card issuers or networks could reduce:

> “revenues from our co-branded credit card agreements”  
> and could result in  
> “reduced program funding.”

**Technology and systems, pp. 16–18**

Marriott identifies its reservation, customer-relationship-management, and Loyalty Program systems as critical technologies. It is undertaking a multi-year transformation of its reservations, property-management, and loyalty systems. The company says most related technology spending is expected to be reimbursed over time, although the filing does not separately identify the portion related to Bonvoy.

**Tax disclosure, p. 50**

Marriott reports a deferred tax asset associated with the Loyalty Program of:

- **$343 million at year-end 2025**
- **$313 million at year-end 2024**

**Executive/strategic context, p. 8**

Marriott describes Marriott Bonvoy as central to its business strategy. It encompasses:

- Marriott’s brand portfolio;
- other travel offerings;
- direct channels; and
- the travel loyalty program.

The company also says its direct digital channels provide members with exclusive offers, rates, and Loyalty Program perks (p. 8)."}

{"results":"## Wyndham Rewards loyalty disclosures in the FY2025 Form 10-K

### 1. Loyalty-member share of check-ins

**Part I, Item 1—Business, “Our Guest Loyalty Program,” p. 5**

- Wyndham states: **“Wyndham Rewards has over 122 million enrolled members.”**
- It further states: **“Our members accounted for over 37% of check-ins at our hotels globally and over 53% in the United States.”**

**Denominators and period:**

| Metric | Numerator | Denominator disclosed in the filing | Period stated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global check-ins | Check-ins by Wyndham Rewards members | **All check-ins at Wyndham hotels globally** | The filing presents the statistic in the FY2025 Business section, but does **not separately specify a date or measurement period** for the percentage |
| U.S. check-ins | Check-ins by Wyndham Rewards members | **All check-ins at Wyndham hotels in the United States** | Same limitation: no separate date or period is stated for the percentage |

The filing does **not** provide the underlying numerical check-in counts, so the exact denominators are described only as the total global and U.S. hotel check-ins, respectively.

The same paragraph says total membership **grew 7% in 2025 and 24% since the end of 2022**.

---

### 2. Membership, member benefits and program scope

**Part I, Item 1—Business, “Our Guest Loyalty Program,” p. 5**

- Wyndham Rewards is described as the Company’s guest loyalty program supporting its portfolio of brands.
- Members earn points for each **qualified stay at participating properties**.
- Points may be redeemed for stays at **thousands of hotels, vacation club resorts and vacation rentals globally**, as well as:
  - experiences;
  - merchandise;
  - gift cards;
  - airline rewards;
  - charitable donations; and
  - tours and activities.
- Wyndham says affiliation with the program encourages members to allocate more travel spending to Wyndham hotels.
- Franchisees benefit through repeat stays, while members benefit through free-night stays and other redemption options.

**Part I, Item 1—Business, “Human Rights,” p. 8**

- Wyndham again refers to **over 122 million enrolled Wyndham Rewards members**.
- Wyndham Rewards and its members have donated **over 225 million points since inception** to nonprofit organizations, including points redeemed for travel and related goods and services.
- The Company specifically states that Wyndham donates Wyndham Rewards points to Polaris to provide victims of human trafficking with temporary safe housing.

**Part I, Item 7—MD&A, “Our Strategy,” p. 6**

- One strategic objective is to **“offer a robust loyalty rewards program to drive guest retention and engagement.”**
- Another is to capture ancillary revenue growth by enhancing **co-branded credit card offerings**, introducing new products and services, and strengthening partnerships and affiliations.

**Part I, Item 1A—Risk Factors, p. 14**

- Wyndham identifies its ability to successfully market its current or future hotel brands and programs, **“including our rewards program,”** as an operating risk.

**Part I, Item 1A—Risk Factors, p. 15**

- The Company says its ability to generate ancillary revenue may be affected by:
  - credit-card-holder spending levels;
  - enrollment rates under the co-branded credit-card program;
  - changes in applicable laws and regulations; and
  - changes to credit-card payment-network rules, policies, guidelines or standards.
- It also says that revenue from partnerships and affiliates depends on guest engagement and the success of third parties’ business models.

---

## 3. Funding and economic mechanisms

### A. Overall program funding and use of funds

**Part I, Item 1—Business, “Our Guest Loyalty Program,” p. 5**

Wyndham states:

> “The program is funded by contributions from eligible revenues generated by Wyndham Rewards members and collected by us from hotels in our system.”

The filing says those funds are applied to:

1. **reimburse hotels and partners for Wyndham Rewards point redemptions** by loyalty members;
2. pay **administrative expenses**; and
3. pay for **marketing initiatives** supporting the program.

This is the principal high-level description of the program’s economic funding model.

---

### B. Fees charged to hotels for member stays and reimbursement economics

**Note 2—Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, “Loyalty Program,” p. F-10**

- Members primarily earn points by staying at hotels operated under Wyndham brands.
- For a member stay at a participating hotel or affiliate property, Wyndham earns revenue from **“a fee charged by the Company to the property owner or manager.”**
- The fee is based on **a percentage of the room revenues generated from the member’s stay**.
- Wyndham recognizes that revenue, **net of redemptions**, over time based on loyalty-point redemption patterns, including estimates of points that will expire or never be redeemed.
- The filing does **not disclose the percentage rate** used for this loyalty-specific fee.

**Note 3—Revenue Recognition, p. F-14**

- Wyndham describes the loyalty fee as a fee charged to a franchised or managed hotel based on **a percentage of room revenues generated from a Wyndham Rewards member’s stay**.
- The fees are intended to reimburse Wyndham for:
  - member redemptions; and
  - activities associated with administering and marketing the program.
- Loyalty fees are treated as variable consideration and recognized **net of redemptions over time**, based on point-redemption patterns, including estimates of points that will expire or never be redeemed.

**General franchisee fee framework—Part I, Item 1—Business, p. 5; Note 3, p. F-14**

- Direct franchisees generally pay:
  - royalties of approximately **5% of gross room revenue**; and
  - marketing and reservation fees of **2% to 4% of gross room revenue**.
- The filing separately describes the loyalty fee as a percentage of member-generated room revenue, but does not state whether that loyalty fee is included in, or charged in addition to, the general marketing and reservation fee range.
- More generally, marketing and reservation fees reimburse Wyndham for centralized reservations, e-commerce channels, third-party distribution, advertising, marketing, sales efforts, operations support, training and related services.
- Wyndham is generally contractually obligated to spend the marketing and reservation fees collected from franchisees on those purposes. **Note 8, p. F-20**, repeats that the Company is generally contractually obligated to use the fees for centralized, brand-specific reservation systems, advertising, promotional and co-marketing programs, and training.

---

### C. Point redemption costs, breakage and loyalty liabilities

**Part I, Item 7—MD&A, “Critical Accounting Estimates and Policies—Loyalty Program,” p. 37**

- As members earn points, Wyndham records a liability for estimated future redemption costs.
- The liability is based on:
  1. an estimated **cost per point**; and
  2. an estimated **redemption rate for the points earned**.
- The redemption-rate estimate is developed with assistance from a **third-party actuarial firm**, using historical experience, current trends and actuarial analysis.
- The Company estimates points that will expire or never be redeemed.
- Management judgment is required in estimating both cost per point and redemption rate; changes could materially affect the recorded liability and results of operations.

**Note 2—Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, p. F-10**

- Wyndham projects the timing of future redemptions using historical redemption levels.
- The estimate includes points expected to expire or never be redeemed and points members are expected eventually to redeem.
- The recorded liability was:

| Date | Total loyalty liability | Current portion | Non-current portion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| December 31, 2025 | **$118 million** | **$73 million** in accrued expenses and other current liabilities | **$45 million** in other non-current liabilities |
| December 31, 2024 | **$105 million** | **$65 million** | **$40 million** |

**Consolidated Balance Sheet and Note 9, pp. F-7 and F-21**

- Deferred revenues totaled **$354 million** at December 31, 2025.
- The balance sheet included **$73 million of accrued loyalty program liabilities** in current liabilities.
- Note 9 identifies accrued loyalty liabilities of **$73 million in 2025**, compared with **$65 million in 2024**.

**Critical Audit Matter—Deferred Revenues and Liability—Wyndham Rewards Loyalty Program, pp. F-2–F-4**

The auditors describe the program as one in which members earn points redeemable for free nights or other rewards. The critical estimates are:

- estimated cost per point;
- estimated overall redemption rate; and
- points expected to expire or never be redeemed.

The auditors used historical redemptions, member behavior, industry forecasts and actuarial specialists to evaluate the estimates.

---

### D. Co-branded credit-card economics

**Part I, Item 7—MD&A, “Critical Accounting Estimates and Policies—Loyalty Program,” p. 37**

- Members also earn points by purchasing everyday services and products with the **Wyndham Rewards co-branded credit card**.
- Wyndham earns revenue related to points issued under the program and recognizes it, net of redemptions, over time based on redemption patterns and estimated expiration/non-redemption.

**Note 2—Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, p. F-10**

- Wyndham earns revenue based on **a percentage of member spending on the Wyndham Rewards co-branded credit cards**.
- The revenue is paid to Wyndham by a **third-party issuing bank**.
- The Company primarily recognizes that revenue over time based on redemption patterns of the points earned, including points expected to expire or never be redeemed.

**Note 3—Revenue Recognition, p. F-14**

- Co-branded-card revenue is generated primarily by:
  - cardholder spending; and
  - enrollment of new cardholders.
- Advance payments from the program are recorded as a contract liability.
- The program primarily contains two performance obligations:
  1. **brand-performance services**, recognized straight-line over the contract term; and
  2. **issuance and redemption of loyalty points**, recognized over time based on redemption patterns, including estimated breakage.

**Deferred co-branded-card revenue—Note 3, p. F-15**

| Date | Deferred co-branded credit-card revenue |
|---|---:|
| December 31, 2025 | **$98 million** |
| December 31, 2024 | **$22 million** |

The filing says the deferred amount represents payments received in advance from co-branded credit-card partners, primarily for card-member activity.

Remaining performance obligations for the **$98 million** at December 31, 2025 were:

- 2026: **$51 million**
- 2027: **$11 million**
- 2028: **$11 million**
- Thereafter: **$25 million**

**Note 3, p. F-16**

- Partnership fees were **$96 million in 2025**, $69 million in 2024 and $65 million in 2023.
- The filing states that partnership fees relate to third-party partnership agreements, **including the co-branded credit-card program**.
- The table separately reports **loyalty revenue of $91 million in 2025**, $69 million in 2024 and $91 million in 2023.

**Part I, Item 7—MD&A, p. 30**

- Net revenues increased by $21 million in 2025 versus 2024, primarily due in part to **$41 million of higher ancillary revenues from growth in the co-branded credit-card program**.
- Higher operating expenses in 2025 included higher costs associated with growth in that program.

---

### E. Loyalty revenue and expense presentation

**Consolidated Statements of Income, p. F-5**

- “Marketing, reservation and loyalty” revenue was reported together:
  - 2025: **$562 million**
  - 2024: **$563 million**
  - 2023: **$578 million**
- “Marketing, reservation and loyalty” expense was reported together:
  - 2025: **$565 million**
  - 2024: **$564 million**
  - 2023: **$569 million**

These combined line items do **not** isolate Wyndham Rewards revenue or expense.

**Note 3—Disaggregation of Net Revenues, p. F-16**

The filing separately disaggregates:

- loyalty revenue: **$91 million in 2025**, $69 million in 2024 and $91 million in 2023;
- marketing and reservation fees: **$471 million in 2025**, $467 million in 2024 and $487 million in 2023; and
- partnership fees, including co-branded-card fees: **$96 million in 2025**, $69 million in 2024 and $65 million in 2023.

---

### F. Deferred loyalty revenue and recognition timing

**Note 3—Deferred Revenues, pp. F-15–F-16**

- Deferred loyalty-program revenue was:
  - **$91 million at December 31, 2025**; and
  - **$97 million at December 31, 2024**.
- It represents loyalty-program fees charged to franchisees, **net of redemption costs**, that have been deferred and will be recognized over time based on point-redemption patterns.

The remaining performance obligations for the **$91 million** deferred loyalty revenue at December 31, 2025 were:

- 2026: **$56 million**
- 2027: **$25 million**
- 2028: **$8 million**
- Thereafter: **$2 million**

---

### G. Former Parent and affiliate arrangements involving Wyndham Rewards

**Note 17—Transactions with Former Parent, p. F-36**

- In connection with the 2018 spin-off, Wyndham and its former Parent, now Travel + Leisure Co., entered into long-term exclusive license agreements intended to retain the former Parent’s affiliations with Wyndham Rewards.
- The agreements also provide for inventory-sharing and customer cross-sell initiatives.
- Wyndham recorded revenue for activities associated with the Wyndham Rewards program of:
  - **$17 million in 2025**
  - **$19 million in 2024**
  - **$15 million in 2023**
- Separately, Wyndham recorded license fees from the former Parent of $101 million, $94 million and $90 million in 2025, 2024 and 2023, respectively. Those amounts are described as license fees under the license, development and noncompetition agreement; the filing separately identifies the $17 million/$19 million/$15 million as revenue from Wyndham Rewards activities.

---

### H. 2025 restructuring affecting loyalty operations

**Part II, Item 7—MD&A, “Restructuring,” p. 32; Note 16, p. F-34**

- In the second quarter of 2025, Wyndham approved a restructuring plan focused primarily on streamlining its **marketing, reservation and loyalty functions**.
- The Company incurred **$16 million of restructuring expenses**, including $8 million related to closing a leased call-center facility in Canada.
- Wyndham expects annualized savings of approximately **$15 million**, primarily in marketing, reservation and loyalty expenses, to be reinvested in other revenue-generating activities."}

It also receives fees from a co-branded-card issuing bank based on card spending and new-card enrollment. |

### Marriott Bonvoy

Marriott’s FY2025 Form 10-K says that approximately **75% of U.S. room nights** and approximately **68% of global room nights** were booked by loyalty-program members. Marriott does not provide the underlying room-night counts or a Bonvoy membership total in the 10-K.

The economic model is unusually broad:

- Hotel owners and other participating properties reimburse Marriott for loyalty-program costs, including marketing, promotion, communications and member services, generally **with no added markup**. Contributions are generally based on a portion of qualified member spend when points are earned.
- Marriott recognizes the related contribution when the points are redeemed, generally net of redemption cost and estimated point breakage.
- Co-branded cards are a major source of funding. Marriott receives fixed payments and variable payments tied principally to card usage, points purchased, free-night certificates and gift cards. The agreements also pay Marriott for licensing its brand and marketing lists and for arranging rewards redemptions.
- Members can earn points through hotel stays, co-branded-card spending and a wide range of partners and travel offerings, while redeeming them across hotels, airlines, rental cars, merchandise, gift cards and experiences.

The Bonvoy loyalty liability was **$7,992 million at December 31, 2025**, reflecting the scale of the outstanding points obligation. That liability is not itself an economic benefit, but it demonstrates the size of the member currency and the future engagement it can generate.

### Wyndham Rewards

Wyndham reports that Wyndham Rewards had **over 122 million enrolled members** and that members accounted for **over 53% of U.S. check-ins** and **over 37% of global check-ins**. The filing presents these statistics in the FY2025 Business section but does not separately specify the measurement period for the percentages; therefore, they should not be treated as perfectly identical to Marriott’s explicitly stated FY2025 room-night statistics.

Wyndham’s funding model is more directly described as a pass-through or cost-recovery model:

- A loyalty fee is charged to the hotel owner or manager as a percentage of room revenue generated by a Rewards member’s stay.
- Loyalty fees are recognized net of redemptions and are intended to reimburse member redemptions plus program administration and marketing.
- Wyndham also receives co-branded-card revenue from a third-party issuing bank, based on member card spending and enrollment. FY2025 partnership fees were **$96 million**, and separately disclosed loyalty revenue was **$91 million**; the filing cautions that some reported revenue and expense lines combine loyalty with marketing and reservations.
- At year-end 2025, Wyndham’s loyalty-program liability was **$118 million**, substantially smaller than Marriott’s, consistent with the difference in company scale and program economics.

## Which appears better positioned for durable economic advantage?

**Marriott appears better positioned.** The conclusion is based on the disclosures, not on valuation or an investment recommendation.

1. **Higher engagement and stronger direct-booking relevance.** Bonvoy members generated approximately **75% of Marriott’s U.S. room nights and 68% globally**, versus Wyndham Rewards members’ **over 53% of U.S. check-ins and over 37% globally**. Even allowing for the room-night/check-in measurement difference, Marriott shows materially greater loyalty penetration, particularly outside the United States.

2. **More diversified monetization.** Marriott combines hotel-owner contributions with a large, international co-branded-card platform, partner activity, licensing and multiple redemption channels. Its filing explicitly calls card payments a significant funding source. Wyndham also has card and partner revenue, but describes its core loyalty economics more narrowly as fees collected from member-generated hotel revenue and used to cover redemption, administrative and marketing costs.

3. **Greater ability to spread fixed program assets.** Marriott’s larger global brand portfolio, member currency, direct digital channels, redemption ecosystem and card relationships can reinforce one another: more members improve card economics and booking conversion, while more properties and redemption choices increase the usefulness of Bonvoy points. That network effect is a plausible source of durable advantage.

4. **More evidence of economic scale.** Marriott’s $7.99 billion loyalty liability indicates a much larger loyalty currency and activity base than Wyndham’s $118 million liability. The liability is a future obligation and should not be confused with profit, but its magnitude supports the inference that Marriott has a deeper member ecosystem and more embedded engagement.

**Important qualification:** Both companies largely design loyalty funding to reimburse redemption and program costs rather than to create a high-margin standalone profit stream. Marriott’s 10-K says centralized programs are generally intended to be reimbursed over the long term and are not designed to affect Marriott’s economics positively or negatively. The durable advantage is therefore more likely to arise indirectly—from repeat stays, direct distribution, customer data, switching costs, pricing/occupancy support and card-partner economics—rather than from reported loyalty revenue alone.

tools.description:
This tool allows you to retrieve data from previously saved documents from the agent's data storage system, by applying an LLM prompt to the stored document.

To use the tool, you will need to provide a prompt. This prompt will include both the query to be sent to the LLM, as well as the keys of files you have previously saved to the data storage system.

For example, if you want to analyze data stored under the key "financial_report", your prompt should look like the following:
"Analyze the following financial report and extract the revenue figures: {{financial_report}}"

The {{key_name}} will be replaced with the full text of the document stored under that key before the query is sent.

IMPORTANT: Your prompt MUST include at least one key from the data storage using this exact format: {{key_name}}. If you don't use this exact format with double braces, the tool will fail to retrieve the information.

You can also optionally only pass *a portion* of each document to the LLM, rather than the entire document. This can be used to avoid token limit errors or improve efficiency. To do so, use the input_character_ranges parameter to specify which portions of documents to extract. For example, if "financial_report" contains "Annual Report 2023" and you specify:  [{"key": "financial_report", "start": 1, "end": 6}], then only "nnual" will be inserted into the prompt (characters 1 through 5, as end is exclusive).

Each object should have 'key' (the document key), 'start' (start character index, inclusive), and 'end' (end character index, exclusive). By default, the full document is used if this parameter is not provided or if a key is not included in the list.

key.description: The document key from data storage

prompt.description: The prompt that will be passed to the LLM. You MUST include at least one data storage key in the format {{key_name}} - for example: 'Summarize this 10-K filing: {{company_10k}}'. The content stored under each key will replace the {{key_name}} placeholder.

tools.description:
This tool allows you to retrieve data from previously saved documents from the agent's data storage system, by applying an LLM prompt to the stored document.

To use the tool, you will need to provide a prompt. This prompt will include both the query to be sent to the LLM, as well as the keys of files you have previously saved to the data storage system.

For example, if you want to analyze data stored under the key "financial_report", your prompt should look like the following:
"Analyze the following financial report and extract the revenue figures: {{financial_report}}"

The {{key_name}} will be replaced with the full text of the document stored under that key before the query is sent.

IMPORTANT: Your prompt MUST include at least one key from the data storage using this exact format: {{key_name}}. If you don't use this exact format with double braces, the tool will fail to retrieve the information.

You can also optionally only pass *a portion* of each document to the LLM, rather than the entire document. This can be used to avoid token limit errors or improve efficiency. To do so, use the input_character_ranges parameter to specify which portions of documents to extract. For example, if "financial_report" contains "Annual Report 2023" and you specify:  [{"key": "financial_report", "start": 1, "end": 6}], then only "nnual" will be inserted into the prompt (characters 1 through 5, as end is exclusive).

You can use the retrieve_information tool to later retrieve information about the stored page.

tools.name: edgar_search

ciks.description: (optional) Filters results to filings from specified CIKs, type list of strings. Leading zeros are optional but may be included. Example: [ "0001811414", "1318605" ]. Default: all CIKs

end_date.description: (optional) End date for the search range, in the same format as startDate. If the value is a date that is later than 2026-03-01, it will be set to 2026-03-01.

form_types.description: (optional) Limits search to specific EDGAR form types (e.g., ['8-K', '10-Q']) list of strings. Default: all form types

page.description: (optional) Used for pagination. Each page contains up to 100 matching filings. Increase the page number to retrieve the next set of 100 filings. Example: 3 retrieves the third page. Default: 1

search_query.description: The case-insensitive search-term or phrase to search the contents of filings and their attachments. This can be a single word, phrase, or combination of words and phrases. Supported search features include wildcards (*), Boolean operators (OR, NOT), and exact phrase matching by enclosing phrases in quotation marks ("exact phrase"). By default, all terms are joined by an implicit AND operator.

start_date.description: (optional) Start date for the search range in yyyy-mm-dd format. If the value is a date that is later than 2026-03-01, it will be set to 2026-03-01.

top_n_results.description: (optional) Return only the first N results out of 100 from the page. If not provided, all 100 results will be returned. E.g. if page is 2, and top_n_results is 10, you will receive results 100 to 110.

tools.description: Search the EDGAR Database through the SEC API. You should provide a search query. You can also optionally provide a start date, an end date, a page number, top N results, a list of form types, and/or a list of CIKs. The results are returned as a list of dictionaries, each containing the metadata for a filing. It does not contain the full text of the filing.

Supports: +, -, *, /, ** (exponentiation), % (modulo), and parentheses for grouping. Available functions: abs(), min(), max(), sqrt(), log(), log10(). Examples: '(5000 - 3200) * 0.21', '(2865507 / 1905871) ** 0.5 - 1', '14060 / 2148'.

asset_class.description: Asset class used to route to the proper pricing endpoint.

end_date.description: End date YYYY-MM-DD (inclusive).

start_date.description: Start date YYYY-MM-DD (inclusive).

ticker.description: Ticker symbol. High-level symbology rules: (1) Equity/ETF/mutual fund: use the US exchange-listed symbol (AAPL, SPY, VFIAX). Symbols are case-insensitive and contain only letters and dashes. (2) Share classes use a dash, not a dot: 'BRK-A' / 'BRK-B' (not 'BRK.A'), 'BF-B'. (3) Securities are identified by the ticker as listed on the primary US exchange; non-US listings, OTC pink sheets, indices, and futures are generally not covered. (4) Tickers can be reused after delisting; data is point-in-time for the entity that held the ticker on each date. (5) Crypto: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'btcusd', 'ethusd'. (6) FX: concatenated lowercase pair with no separator, e.g. 'audusd', 'eurusd'.

tools.description: Fetch historical daily price data for a specific asset class. Returns a CSV table with one row per day. Use asset_class='equity' or 'etf' for US-listed stocks/ETFs (e.g. AAPL, SPY), 'crypto' for pairs like btcusd (lowercase, no dash), or 'fx' for pairs like audusd. Non-US equities and most indices/futures are not covered by the pricing provider. Each row includes raw OHLC (open/high/low/close), split- and dividend-adjusted OHLC (adjOpen/adjHigh/adjLow/adjClose), raw and adjusted volume, divCash (dividend amount on the date), and splitFactor.
